ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The erector spinae is a group of back muscles that straighten and rotate the spine. They are key for posture, movement, and protecting the spinal column. Dysfunction can cause pain, limited mobility, and posture problems.

sections.p: The erector spinae consists of three parallel muscle columns that run from the pelvis to the skull. They are essential for maintaining upright posture and facilitating spinal movements.
The muscles originate from the sacrum, iliac crest, and thoracic vertebrae, inserting on the ribs, transverse processes, and skull. They are arranged from lateral to medial.
They lie deep to the trapezius and latissimus dorsi, superficial to the vertebral column and intervertebral discs. They are adjacent to the sympathetic chain.
Supplied by branches of the lumbar, thoracic, and cervical arteries.
Innervated by the dorsal rami of spinal nerves from T1 to L5.
Primary actions are extension, lateral flexion, and rotation of the spine. They also stabilize the vertebral column during movement.
Common issues include muscle strain, myofascial pain, and lumbar spine disorders. In low-resource settings, infections like tuberculosis can involve the erector spinae.

t.b: Detects muscle edema, abscess, or spinal involvement; abnormal signal indicates inflammation or infection
Shows vertebral alignment; loss of lordosis suggests muscle dysfunction
Elevated WBC may indicate infection; normal CBC does not rule out local muscle infection

sections.p: Ask about pain during extension or rotation. Palpate for tenderness along the spinous processes. Inquire about recent heavy lifting or trauma.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe back pain with fever, weight loss, or neurological deficits (e.g., weakness, numbness)

faq.q: What causes acute back pain in the erector spinae?
faq.a: Overuse, heavy lifting, sudden twisting, or poor posture can strain these muscles.

faq.q: Can infections affect the erector spinae?
faq.a: Yes, spinal tuberculosis or abscesses can involve the muscles, especially in endemic areas.

faq.q: How is a muscle strain diagnosed?
faq.a: Clinical exam plus imaging (MRI) if red flags present; otherwise, history and physical are sufficient.
